analysis.one_liner: Makes online marketplaces financially liable when third-party sellers on them offer counterfeit health-and-safety goods.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with one Republican cosponsor, got a single subcommittee hearing, and never received a Senate vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The SHOP SAFE Act would let trademark holders sue large online marketplaces — like Amazon or eBay — when third-party sellers use their platforms to sell counterfeit products that could hurt someone, such as fake car seats, cosmetics, or medicine. Marketplaces could avoid that liability by taking specific steps: verifying sellers, screening listings proactively, quickly removing flagged fakes, and banning repeat counterfeiters. The bill never advanced past a subcommittee hearing.
analysis.who_benefits: Shoppers who buy goods online, who would face fewer dangerous fakes, plus the trademark-owning brands whose products are copied. Third-party sellers of legitimate goods also gain from a marketplace with fewer counterfeit competitors.

how_it_helps.text: Gives a legal remedy against large e-commerce platforms for counterfeit goods that implicate health and safety, putting the responsibility for policing fakes on the marketplace rather than only on the brand or the injured buyer [S2].

Requires platforms above $500,000 in annual sales to take concrete steps before liability applies: verify sellers, screen listings before they go live at no charge to brand owners, remove flagged listings quickly, and terminate sellers with repeated counterfeits [S2].
Gives brand owners and consumers an accessible way to report suspected counterfeits and requires platforms to make seller contact information available so counterfeiters can be pursued [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large online marketplaces, which would bear screening, verification, and removal costs and face lawsuits if counterfeit health-and-safety goods sell on their sites. Those costs would likely be passed on partly to sellers in fees and partly to shoppers in prices, and some legitimate listings could get swept up in screening before being reinstated.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large e-commerce marketplaces and their sellers

drawbacks.text: The definition of a 'good that implicates health and safety' is extremely broad — any consumer product that 'can lead to illness, disease, injury, serious adverse event, allergic reaction, or death' if made improperly — which covers most physical goods and could drive aggressive over-removal of legitimate listings [S2].

Compliance costs fall on platforms and would likely be passed through to third-party sellers as fees; small businesses selling online would bear some of that even though they are not the counterfeiters [S2].
The 'reasonable measures' safe harbor gives courts wide discretion to judge platforms by their size and resources, which could produce inconsistent outcomes between large and small marketplaces [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: shoppers cannot easily tell a genuine car seat or medicine from a counterfeit, and putting policing duty on the platform that profits from the sale is a workable design. The main cost is over-removal risk and compliance fees passed to honest sellers, which the bill tries to limit with reinstatement and appeal procedures. On balance a consumer-protection bill with manageable, though real, side costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, got one subcommittee hearing on intellectual property, was never brought up for a committee or floor vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Christopher Coons (D-DE), joined by Sen. Tillis, introduced the bill on September 26, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Judiciary Committee [S1][S4].
It attracted only two cosponsors, one Republican and one Democrat [S3].

The Judiciary Subcommittee on Intellectual Property held a hearing on October 3, 2023 [S4], but the bill was never reported out of committee or scheduled for a Senate vote before the 118th Congress ended [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large online marketplaces — which avoided new liability and screening obligations — and counterfeit sellers, who continued to face only the old, harder-to-enforce rules. Shoppers remain exposed to counterfeit health-and-safety goods.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large online marketplaces and counterfeit sellers

industries.industry: Large online marketplaces (Amazon, eBay, and similar third-party seller platforms)
industries.note: The bill makes them financially liable for counterfeit health-and-safety goods sold by third parties unless they meet a list of screening and removal requirements, creating significant compliance costs and lawsuit exposure. Their interest in defeating the bill ran against shoppers' interest in fewer fakes.
They gain a practical tool to shut down counterfeiters, since platforms must screen for their marks at no charge. This benefit runs alongside shoppers' interest in genuine, safe goods.

industries.industry: Third-party online sellers of legitimate goods
industries.note: They face new requirements (verified U.S. addresses, accurate product images) and risk having listings blocked pending proof of authenticity, but they also benefit when counterfeit competitors are cleared off the platform.
The bill cuts off their main sales channel by requiring platforms to terminate repeat counterfeiters and block re-entry under new aliases. Their loss is the public's gain.
